learn.title: Look at every item
learn.body: Searching means finding where a value sits in a collection, or learning that it is not there. The simplest way is linear search: start at the first item and check each one in turn until you find it or run out.

learn.title: Linear search in C
learn.body: It returns the index of the target, or -1 when the target is missing. An index is never negative, so -1 is a safe signal for not found.

learn.title: Searching {7, 3, 9, 1, 5} for 5
steps: Searching for 4 would check all five items and return -1

learn.title: What it costs
learn.body: In the worst case linear search checks all n items, so it is $O(n)$. In the best case the target is first, so it is $O(1)$. It works on any array, sorted or not, and that is its strength.
Return inside the loop as soon as you find the target. Do not report -1 until the whole loop has finished.

questions.prompt: What does `linear` return when the target is not in the array?
questions.explanation: -1 can never be a valid index, so it signals not found. 0 would look like the first item.
4 is not in the array, so the loop ends and the function returns -1.

questions.prompt: In the worst case linear search makes \_\_ comparisons for n items.
questions.explanation: It might have to look at every item.

questions.prompt: Does linear search need the array to be sorted?
choices: No, it works on any order
questions.explanation: It checks items one by one, so the order does not matter.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of linear search in order.
steps: Compare the item with the target
questions.explanation: Check each item, stop on a match, and only give up at the end.

questions.prompt: If the target is the first item, how many comparisons does linear search make?
questions.explanation: It stops straight away. That is the best case.
